name: Rosa Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck team and use the mine's approved AI dashboard to spot odd engine-heat patterns before a shift. I mark each warning on a laminated orange route card, then walk the newer drivers around the loading face so they can compare the map with the ground.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you in the job, and what do you find hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like finding a problem early and getting the crew to fix it together. My pay is high for the job, I have more than six months saved, and there are plenty of mines nearby, so I can afford to ask whether a new tool is actually useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a small AI tool can tidy the maintenance notes if the crew still checks each warning. I still verify every heat warning against the radio before a driver moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving work and pay look secure in this mild version, because most of my shift is physical. I have a strong cushion and several nearby mines, so I can test the tool without treating it as a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same crew rotation and compare the dashboard's heat warnings with the orange route card. I would keep using the tool for routine notes only when it matched the radio log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job and income in this picture. If the tool catches a warning early without changing the crew's safety routine, I see no reason to fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful test of the new notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a month's heat alerts with the mechanic's service record and count which warnings led to a real inspection. If the summary hid a fault, I would stop using it for that task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should get the final say if the dashboard and a driver disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The driver who sees the road should be able to pause the truck while the crew checks. I would ask the union safety contact to make that rule clear before another tool is added.

I still verify heat alerts against **radio calls** before a driver moves.
think: I think my driving work and pay look **secure** in this picture.
My savings let me **test the tool** without rushing.
do: Keep the **same crew rotation** and compare heat warnings with the route card.
Use AI notes only when they match the **radio log**.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own job and income in this mild case.
S0.quote: I still verify every heat warning against the radio before a driver moves.
fieldNote: Rosa uses the dashboard for **early warning**, while keeping the driver in control.
Her high pay and **strong savings** make the mild scenario financially secure.
She wants a **month-long comparison** with actual service records.

steps.text: Keep the crew rotation and compare dashboard alerts with the route card
Check AI heat alerts against the mechanic's service record

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Software can draft the route, but I still own the call when the road changes. I would tell the company to publish whether it plans to change lead hours when route planning and maintenance reports move to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the approved dashboard every day, so I am not worried about learning another tool after the crew tests it. I am uneasy that the mine could remove lead hours while still asking the remaining operators to check more routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would log where the new planner agrees or disagrees with the orange route card for a month. If it proves useful, I would learn its maintenance-report feature during paid time and ask the union to keep a human safety override.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about my lead duties changing, but the truck work still looks stable for now. I would check the rota and pay slip before assuming a planning tool had cut my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which change would tell you that your own hours were being reduced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a missing lead name on the rota or less paid handover time. If that happened, I would bring the figures to the union meeting and ask for a paid course before the next schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI recommends a route you would not use, how would you handle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the ground, radio and hazard card, then show the planner's route to another operator. If both of us saw the same problem, I would file the mismatch for the system team and use the safe route.

say: Software can draft routes, but I own the **call when roads change**.
I would ask the company to publish changes to **lead hours**.
think: I am comfortable learning a tool after the **crew tests it**.
I worry the mine may remove lead hours but add **review work**.
do: Log planner differences against the **orange route card** for a month.
Learn report features on paid time and request a **human safety override**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about changing lead duties, though truck work remains steady.
S1.quote: Software can draft the route, but I still own the call when the road changes.
fieldNote: Rosa separates **software suggestions** from responsibility for the road.
Her concern is **unpaid checking work** if lead duties are reduced.

steps.text: Log planner differences against the orange route card

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain that thinking AI comes first and robots follow about three years later. I would ask the mine to post real training places and wages instead of telling everyone that a transition will work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my haul-truck hours could shrink by 2031 because robots can do the hands-on task I am paid for. I have more than six months saved and many nearby mines, but I would rather move early than compete for the same jobs after a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union to secure paid training in physical equipment inspection and enroll if a place opened. In 2029, after thinking AGI arrives, I would apply for inspection work only if the job involved physical checks and a wage that matched my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could replace my main paid task within five years. My savings and local options give me control, so I would train or move before I had to make a rushed decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection post is mainly records and planning, which AGI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not treat the post as a protected job, because AGI can handle those thinking tasks. I would ask which parts require physical checks and how many people the mine expects to hire after the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine cannot say how many posts remain or what they pay, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current job while checking the union's figures and other mines' openings. I would not leave a high-paying crew role for an inspection title without a clear wage and duration.

I would ask for actual **training places and wages**.
think: My truck hours could shrink by **2031**.
My savings and nearby mines give me a real option to **move early**.
do: Ask the union to secure paid **physical inspection training**.

S2.quote: I expect my haul-truck hours could shrink by 2031 because robots can do the hands-on task I am paid for.
fieldNote: Rosa expects a **specific earnings threat** by the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the mine to start paid apprenticeships before the planning work changes. I would also ask the union to negotiate notice and fair pay for anyone whose truck role is removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years gives me time to train while my current wage continues, and there are plenty of mines nearby. I would focus on physical inspection rather than records because AGI can handle thinking tasks, but I do not know how many inspection jobs last after 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete a paid equipment-inspection apprenticeship before 2031 and keep my haul-truck qualification current. In 2032, the first year after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection shifts only if the employer named the wage and expected duration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have time and savings to prepare, but no one has shown the mine's staffing plan. I would keep earning while I train instead of leaving my role for an uncertain bridge job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to know before paying for advanced training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether other mines use the certificate for physical inspection and how many people they hired last year. If the work is mostly entering records, I would not spend more on it after AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In 2032, if inspection work is only a short bridge before robots arrive, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it if the wage covered my bills and gave me time to apply elsewhere before 2034. If it did not, I would keep the truck job and use my savings to stay flexible.

say: I would ask for paid apprenticeships before **planning work changes**.
I would negotiate notice and **fair pay** if roles disappear.
think: Eight years lets me train while **my wage continues**.
I need to know if physical inspection lasts after **2034**.
do: In 2032, apply only with stated **wage and duration** from a local employer in writing.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I can prepare, but mine staffing is unknown.
S3.quote: I do not know how many inspection jobs last after 2034.
fieldNote: Rosa sees the five-year warning as **time to train**.
She avoids treating records work as a **fallback after AGI**.
She wants **wages and duration** before accepting physical inspection work.

steps.text: Complete a paid equipment-inspection apprenticeship before 2031
Apply for physical inspection shifts with stated wages in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union and the mine to publish training routes well before 2036. I would also say that the three-year gap before robots is useful time, not proof that physical jobs will remain afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before robots arrive gives me time to build another skill while earning a high wage. I would still check how much physical work remains after 2039 before I moved my career toward maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my job and join the union's transition group to request paid inspection courses and accurate job forecasts. In 2037, after AGI arrives, I would review the physical vacancies and wage information before deciding whether to change mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my income and work look secure for years, and I have savings to prepare. I would rather make a move after seeing a funded training route than worry every day about a date more than a decade away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you need before accepting a maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the work is physical, what it pays and how long the employer expects the role to last. I would also check whether the certificate transfers to other mines if robots arrive sooner than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the job forecast is unclear in 2037, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my current crew and ask the union for updated numbers. I would wait to move until the employer could put a vacancy and wage on paper.

say: I would ask for training routes before **2036**.
I would treat the robot gap as time, not **proof of lasting jobs**.
think: I have thirteen years to build a skill while **earning a high wage**.
I would check physical work after **2039** before changing careers.
do: Join the union transition group and request **paid inspection courses**.
In 2037, review physical vacancies and **wages** before moving.
feel: I feel **calm** because work and income look secure for years.
S4.quote: I would rather make a move after seeing a funded training route than worry every day about a date more than a decade away.
fieldNote: Rosa treats the long lead as **preparation time**, not a guarantee.
She uses the union to request **forecasts and transferable courses**.
Her strong income and savings make a **rushed move unnecessary**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots may reach the truck work by around 2031. Paid training, accurate job forecasts and a fair union agreement would help me choose another role without giving up worker protections.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want the crew to see how a tool works before it gets a vote on safety. A machine can help us spot a problem, but workers need the right to stop when the ground tells us something different.

headlineQuote: I want the crew to see how a tool works before it gets a vote on safety.
portrait: Rosa Young is **27** and leads a haul-truck team at a large mine.
She earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of savings.
Plenty of nearby mines give her **options** if the crew changes.
She uses AI tools daily and checks alerts against the **road and radio**.
She favors union protections and **paid training** while planning around robot exposure.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until about 2031 before robots threaten her truck work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, accurate job forecasts and a fair union agreement would help Rosa move without losing worker protections.
